title: Google’s Gemini 3.8 Flash Matches Frontier Models in Chemistry Test
summary: Google's Gemini 3.8 Flash matches frontier models in chemistry tests
detailed: Google DeepMind released specialized chemistry tools for its Antigravity AI platform on November 25, enabling lightweight Gemini 3.8 Flash to match frontier models like Gemini 4 Argon and Carbon.
When equipped with internet access and Mass Spec Skills, all three models correctly identified exact molecules in about 97% of test attempts across 100 compounds.
Performance dropped sharply without the specialized tools, with Flash missing over three-quarters of attempts using internet access alone and dropping below 4% without any tools.
This matters because specialized tools significantly enhance AI accuracy and token efficiency in complex scientific tasks like tandem mass spectrometry analysis.
sentences: Google DeepMind’s lightweight Gemini 3.8 Flash matched Gemini 4 Argon and Gemini 4 Carbon in identifying known compounds, showing the importance of specialized tools in the chemistry task.
All three models identified the exact molecule in about 97% of attempts when they had internet access, Mass Spec Skills and compounds with public reference spectra.
Google DeepMind released the tools for its Antigravity AI platform on Nov.
The test covered 100 compounds from the Enamine REAL tandem mass spectrometry collection in the public MoNA library.
The structures were also cataloged in PubChem.
Recordings with too few useful molecular fragments were excluded, and each spectrum received three attempts.
Runs taking more than one hour counted as failures, while temporary infrastructure and quota errors were excluded.
Performance fell sharply without the specialized tools.
With internet access alone, Flash missed more than three-quarters of its attempts, while Argon and Carbon missed roughly one-quarter to one-third.
Without internet access or Mass Spec Skills, all three models scored below 4%.
Tandem mass spectrometry identifies compounds by measuring the charged fragments produced when molecules break apart.
The tools help Antigravity clean noisy signals, search reference spectra and compare proposed structures with measured fragments.
The tools also reduced the number of tokens generated per attempt, with the largest proportional reduction reported for Flash.
Flash using the tools was more accurate than either frontier model using internet access alone.
When no usable reference spectrum is available, Antigravity can infer a molecular formula and narrow the list of structures that fit the measured fragments.
In a demonstration without library lookup, it selected a compound already cataloged in PubChem.
That process produces candidates for chemist review rather than independently confirming a new molecule.
Mirror-image molecules and some closely related compounds can produce similar spectra, so additional measurements may be needed to distinguish them.
Simon Yoon reports on blockchain technology for TokenPost.
